summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Entries are now open for the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. The Behaviour Change Campaign of the Year award, sponsored by Clarksons Port Services, celebrates campaigns that have successfully encouraged more sustainable behaviours and delivered a positive environmental impact. Adam Tucker, account manager at Clarksons Port Services, is looking forward to seeing entries that demonstrate genuine and measurable change. “We want to recognise initiatives that inspire people to take action and create lasting, positive behaviour change in support of sustainability,” said Mr Tucker. He explained that the strongest submissions will combine creativity with evidence, demonstrating how innovative ideas, audience insight and effective engagement have influenced behaviours in meaningful ways. “We’re particularly interested in campaigns that not only capture attention but also motivate people to adopt more sustainable habits,” he said. Adam Tucker, account manager at Clarksons Port Services (Image: Clarksons Port Services) Mr Tucker believes behaviour change plays a vital role in addressing environmental challenges and achieving long-term sustainability goals. “While innovation, technology and policy all have an important role to play, lasting environmental improvements ultimately depend on the decisions people make every day,” he said. “Successful sustainability initiatives don’t just inform people; they inspire and enable action.” Innovation and audience engagement will also be important judging criteria, alongside the potential for ideas to be scaled or adapted more widely. Mr Tucker added: “The ability to scale, adapt and inspire change across different communities or sectors is an important part of creating long-term environmental impact. “We’re excited to celebrate the organisations leading the way and recognising campaigns that have the potential to make a difference well beyond their original scope.” The entry deadline for the Behaviour Change Campaign of the Year award is midnight on Sunday, November 8. For more information about the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To read about all of the award categories, please click here. Clarksons Port Services (CPS) is a leading provider of integrated logistics solutions, delivering trusted support to the global maritime industry. The firm combines decades of experience with a global network and deep local expertise to provide tailored services for clients. It operates from strategic locations across the UK and Europe, offering port agency, customs clearance and consultancy, vessel chartering, crew change coordination, project management, helicopter operations, freight forwarding, project logistics, warehousing and storage, bunker supply, quayside logistics management, supply chain management, tooling and supplies, and safety and survival equipment. The judges will be seeking a campaign that has effectively driven positive behaviour change in relation to sustainability. Innovation, audience engagement and measurable changes in behaviour will be key factors. The potential for the campaign to be adapted for wider audiences will also be considered.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP wades in amid claims migrants being housed in Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
An MP has waded in and called for improved communication amid claims migrants are being housed in a Huntingdonshire town. The call follows a statement from government contractor Serco over rumours that asylum seekers were being moved into empty flats in Eynesbury, St Neots. A video shared with The Hunts Post appears to show a housing officer from Serco inspecting the properties on August 13. It is understood the official "confirmed" asylum seekers will move into the addresses, although this could not be independently verified. Concerns have been raised about the suitability of the properties, which are located in close proximity to vulnerable residents. This newspaper has chosen not to identify the exact location of the properties to ensure the safety of those who may live there. The MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire, Ian Sollom, confirmed Serco submitted a nomination for the properties on May 6 this year. This was assessed by "three separate council teams before being supported for family use", he told this newspaper. "What clearly didn't happen is any communication with residents, ward councillors, or me as the local MP," he said. "Finding out about something like this from social media, rather than from any official source, is a bad way to learn what's happening on your own street, and I don't think raising questions about that makes anyone unreasonable." According to Mr Sollom, the Home Office confirmed on August 20 that four family properties had been procured but were not occupied at that time. He urged locals to treat any claims about current occupancy status "with some caution until they're confirmed by the Home Office directly". However, the MP revealed he has seen figures that "don't match what I've been told directly by the Home Office - for instance, the number of properties involved". "That may not be deliberate misinformation," he explained. "It could simply be a symptom of how little official information has reached residents, which is itself part of the problem." Read more Government contractor responds to claims migrants being housed in Hunts
    Reform councillor tables motion to stop further asylum accommodation in Hunts
    LIVE: Cambs leaders react as government halt LGR decisions
    Photos show large turnout at first Capital & Centric consultation in Hunts
    WATCH: 'Disgusting' car park plans slammed by St Neots residents at consultation Moving forward, Mr Sollom said he'd like to see the local authority and representatives "properly looped in before a property is brought into use". "I'd like the Home Office to communicate directly with affected communities rather than leaving residents to find out secondhand," he added. "The contractual process with the council doesn’t include any public-facing communication, and that's the gap I want closed." Councillor Stephen Ferguson said the wider community had not "been given the information they need to plan ahead". He added: "The priority now is for Serco, the council, the police, local services, community groups and residents to work together. "We need to keep everyone safe, make sure the right plans are in place and give people clear facts instead of leaving rumours to spread." "St Neots is a strong and welcoming community. If we share the facts, speak calmly and work together, we can deal with this in a sensible and responsible way." Serco said it does not confirm the addresses of properties it may rent for asylum accommodation. A spokesperson said: "We work under the direction of the Home Office, who decide where people are placed, based on overall national demand." Despite this, Cambridgeshire Constabulary said it had "been notified by partners and are engaging with them". Huntingdonshire District Council said it was aware of "speculation" regarding "potential asylum accommodation in the Eynesbury ward of St Neots". A spokesperson said: "Decisions about asylum accommodation are the responsibility of the Home Office and its accommodation providers. "While the council may be consulted and can raise local concerns where appropriate, it does not make these decisions. "It would not be appropriate for the council to comment on, verify, or speculate about reports relating to specific properties or individuals. They added: "Any confirmation should come from the Home Office or the relevant accommodation provider. "We encourage residents to rely on trusted, official sources and avoid sharing unverified information." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk or newsdesk@huntspost.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 18 prisoners to be released early in Bedfordshire next month
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Eighteen offenders are due for early release in Bedfordshire next month as part of a national programme to ease pressure on prison space, a meeting heard. The probation service will supervise them within the county and is confident it can manage the situation, despite its financial constraints, the Bedfordshire Police and Crime Panel was told. “This has been the county force’s busiest summer for a long time, with significant increases in incidents and cases,” according to Bedfordshire Police and Crime Commissioner John Tizard. “We’ve had a fatal police shooting (in Bedford), a rail crash (near Elstow), five homicides, the process of extraditing the Tate brothers from the United States, and extraditing the suspect from South Africa in respect of one of the homicides,” he explained. “There’ve been a number of other incidents too, as well as the Bedford River Festival which took 150 officers. We’ve 80-plus county lines and a significant number of organised crime syndicates. “The pressures have been quite significant. It’s no excuse for performance, but it’s putting all this into that perspective.” He described the early release of prisoners as having been “a moving position”, saying: “We now know 18 prisoners will be released early in Bedfordshire in October. “They’re known and named, and the probation service will have responsibility for their supervision. The police will be informed of those releases. It puts pressure on the offender management unit. “If there’s a level of recall, the police often have to get involved. The probation service is confident it can manage the position, but it also has resource restraints. “Early release is probably inevitable given the current state of the prison estate across the country. Even if you build new prisons, you can’t build them at the pace required.” There are some areas of significant challenge in terms of overall performance in Bedfordshire, “although we’re moving in the right direction in aspects such as responding to the public”, added the PCC. “The police are consistently achieving 90 per cent and often above of 999 calls answered within ten seconds, which is the national standard. The bigger challenge is getting to ‘immediate cases’, which should be within 15 minutes and where the national standard is 80 per cent plus. “We’re currently well below that. We’re making progress and are in the high 50s (per cent) on a regular basis now, but that has to improve. “Another area is solving crime. A new report says investigating crime is an issue on a national basis. That’s partly because there are insufficient qualified detectives. “Bedfordshire has more of these than a year ago and quite a considerable number in training. The solve rate is better than it was, but there’s still some way to go. “Domestic abuse and domestic violence are a priority and very much a target for the police. We’re making significant improvements in that area, but there’s some way to go. “It’s the repeat offences. We’re using the orders available through the courts to hold the perpetrators to account. That’s an area of great focus.” Asked about progress on police reform, Mr Tizard replied: “The government’s intention is to replace PCC’s with a new form of governance from May 2028. “The ambition is that mayors would take over the role. The Police Reform Bill was due to be presented to Parliament within the last two weeks. “But that’s not happened and the expectation is this legislation won’t be presented for its first reading until January. The government is still saying it aims to achieve the same timetable, although it’s a tight schedule.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Controversial guided busway approved for Cambs
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The government has approved plans for a controversial new busway linking Cambridge and Cambourne. The Cambourne to Cambridge guided busway route, known as C2C, was first proposed in 2014 with a two-month public inquiry finishing in November of last year. There were concerns about safety after the deaths of three people on a different busway in the county between 2015 and 2021. The project is estimated to cost £180m and will run through the century-old Coton Orchard, and has led to more than 300 objections to the route. The plans will be delivered by Cambridgeshire County Council on behalf of the Greater Cambridge Partnership (GCP). The planned route will go via the new Bourn Airfield development, Hardwick, Coton and the university’s Cambridge West site. The GCP said Cambourne is expected to grow “significantly” over the next few years, with plans for up to 13,000 new homes, and hope the busway will provide 10,000 daily passenger trips. The secretary of state approved the plans on Tuesday evening (September 8). Cllr Brian Milnes, chair of the the GCP’s executive board, said that with thousands more homes planned for Cambourne, the route will be a “desperately needed new transport link”. He said: “We all know how difficult it can be for residents to get from Cambourne into Cambridge. “Whilst many objectors wanted Cambourne to Cambridge to take a different route, almost all of them agreed that improved public transport is essential for our area.” Cllr Lucy Nethsingha, leader of Cambridgeshire County Council, said the link would give “tens of thousands of residents” easy access to “low carbon and low congestion transport into Cambridge city”. Cllr Katie Thornburrow, leader of Cambridge City Council, said the route was an “important component” of an “integrated transport solution for the region”. She said: “Offering fast, efficient public transport along with options for active transport like cycling gives everyone more choice. “I am confident this scheme will ease congestion and delays on key routes into the city, improve journey reliability and contribute to better air quality, while supporting sustainable growth for communities both now and in the future.” Cllr Bridget Smith, leader of South Cambridgeshire District Council, said: “It’s vital our growing communities have a reliable, sustainable, and affordable way to travel between Cambourne and the city – giving them a genuine alternative to driving. “It will be particularly transformational for younger residents – giving them better access to Cambridge’s opportunities.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New independent veterinary practice opens in Huntingdon
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new independent veterinary practice has opened in Huntingdon. Huntsbridge Vets welcomed its first clients to its new independent practice at Vantage Park on Tuesday, September 1. This followed a community open day and ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by MP Ben Obese-Jecty. The practice is the result of months of planning and preparation by its four founders, who bring together expertise in veterinary medicine, nursing, management and client care. Julie Eastham, practice manager and one of the founding partners, said: "It has been a huge amount of work bringing our vision for Huntsbridge Vets to life, so seeing the practice open and welcoming our first clients has been incredibly special. Huntsbridge Vets opens its doors in Huntingdon this week (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) "Our open day gave us the opportunity to meet many of the people who will become our clients, but now it’s even more exciting to actually welcome them and their pets through the doors. "Building those relationships and getting to know our clients and their animals is one of the things we have been looking forward to most." The founding team also includes veterinary surgeons Nigel Belgrove and Rachael Day, and registered veterinary nurse Anne Selfe. They say their goal is to provide high-quality veterinary care in a practice that is genuinely connected to the community. Huntsbridge Vets is now open to new clients and pets (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) Huntsbridge Vets has been designed with a modern, welcoming feel, aiming to combine contemporary facilities with a personal approach. Mr Belgrove said: "We have a really passionate team, and we all share the same ambition for Huntsbridge Vets. "We want to provide excellent clinical care, but just as importantly, we want people to feel that they know who is looking after their pets and that they have a veterinary team they can trust." MP Ben Obese-Jecty attends ribbon-cutting at Huntingdon practice (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) Ms Day said the environment was designed with comfort in mind. She said: "Visiting the vets can be stressful for both pets and their owners. Founders Anne, Julie, Nigel and Rachael welcome first clients (Image: Huntsbridge Vets) "We have tried to create an environment that is calm, welcoming and reassuring, while ensuring that we can provide the high standard of veterinary care our patients deserve."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Campaign urges Cambs people to talk openly to help prevent suicide
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The STOP Suicide campaign is urging people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough to spot the signs someone is struggling and start supportive conversations. Ashley Bunn, chief executive of CPSL Mind, said: "On World Suicide Prevention Day, and every day, we must continue to raise awareness about suicide and support people to have open and supportive conversations. "Our new strategy outlines how too many people still only reach support at the point of crisis. "We will continue to work tirelessly to improve access to timely and accessible support in the community, ensuring people access the right support at the right time for them." Denver (Image: Cambridge United Foundation) Led by CPSL Mind and backed by NHS and public health teams, the campaign urges people to spot warning signs, ask directly about suicide and help those at risk stay safe. It highlights that one in four people will experience suicidal thoughts during their lifetime. Fenland has the highest reported suicide rate in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, while Peterborough’s rate is also above the national average. STOP Suicide is sharing personal stories from people who have faced mental health challenges, including Dee from St Neots. In the campaign video, Dee said: "When you go through something so dark and so isolating, there is no hope. "I felt like there was no other solution, I was so ready to end it all." A conversation with a friend’s father changed her perspective, and she hopes the campaign shows others that even a glimpse of hope is possible. STOP Suicide workshops are available to help individuals recognise warning signs, ask about suicide, and support others to stay safe. Find resources and information at www.cpslmind.org.uk. Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 999, while the Samaritans can be contacted on 116 123 for emotional support.

She said: “I hope to see submissions from nominees who can evidence professional development and learning milestones.” Elizabeth Conboy, executive director, commercial at RenewableUK (Image: RenewableUK) Ms Conboy said the award provides an opportunity to celebrate the role apprentices play in driving innovation, skills development and business success. She said: “For apprentices, it offers valuable recognition and helps raise their profile within the industry. “For employers, it showcases their commitment to nurturing talent, investing in future leaders and building the diverse, skilled workforce needed to deliver a more sustainable future.” Discussing the impact the accolade could have, Ms Conboy said: “For the winner and finalists, I hope it will boost confidence, raise their profile, open new career opportunities and strengthen professional networks. “It also highlights the importance of apprenticeships, inspiring others to develop their skills and pursue leadership roles in the transition to a sustainable energy future.” She said exceptional apprentices stand out from their peers with their attitude, curiosity and adaptability. “Outstanding apprentices combine curiosity, initiative and a willingness to learn,” she said. “In a fast-moving sector like renewables, those who demonstrate adaptability, collaboration and a genuine passion for making a positive impact are the ones who truly stand out.” Submit your entries before the deadline, which is midnight on Sunday, November 8. To enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To find out more about all categories, please click here. RenewableUK is the UK’s leading trade association for the renewable energy sector, representing close to 500 members spanning the full supply chain, including offshore wind, onshore wind, energy storage, and wave and tidal power. RenewableUK exists to create and protect the political, commercial and public conditions needed to accelerate the UK’s clean energy transition. The trade association works on behalf of its members to demonstrate that renewable energy delivers energy security, lower bills, investment, jobs and economic growth, while helping remove the barriers that prevent deployment at scale. By connecting industry and policy makers, RenewableUK strengthens the nation’s global leadership in renewables, building a secure, affordable and sustainable energy future. The judges will be looking for an apprentice who has demonstrated exceptional commitment, achievement and personal development. The winner should showcase a strong work ethic, a passion for learning and a positive contribution to their workplace, colleagues and the wider business. Evidence of growth, initiative and the ability to overcome challenges will be key judging factors.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: More than 200 Addenbrooke's Hospital patients harmed, mistaken update reveals
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 200 patients were harmed at a Cambridgeshire hospital according to an interim update that was shared by mistake. Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (CUH) commissioned an external review into the practice of orthopaedic consultant Kuldeep Stohr in 2024 after colleagues raised concerns. Her clinical practice was restricted as a precautionary measure and she remains suspended. A report to the board of CUH, which has since been removed from the hospital’s website, said that of the 924 patients whose care has been reviewed so far, 209 “experienced harm”, the BBC reported. One of the cases was fatal, and 47 were classed as severe. Of the 209 who experienced harm, 139 received elective care when they were children. It was previously reported that nine-year-old Jack Moate died in November 2015, within two months of being operated on by Ms Stohr at Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge. Jack, who had many complex medical needs and limited mobility, spent almost eight hours in surgery for the operation on his hips. The hospital trust said his case had been referred to the coroner. Nicola Ayton, chief executive at Cambridge University Hospitals, said that a “confidential interim update from the external clinical review was shared by mistake in our public board papers”. She said she was “writing to every affected patient and family to apologise and explain what happened”. The paper did not include any patient-identifiable information or any details about individual cases. She continued: “We are deeply sorry to the patients and families who came to harm or experienced care below the standards they should expect. “This should never have happened and we are making changes so that something like this could not happen again.” The external clinical review, chaired by Andrew Kennedy KC, is “due to be completed later this year”, she said. “We have promised that once we receive the final report, which will include confirmed levels of patient harm, we will share it with patients and families first before publishing it in full,” she said. Concerns had been raised as early as 2015 and were the subject of an external clinical review in 2016. A separate independent review, which reported back last year, highlighted how the 2016 review raised concerns about Ms Stohr’s surgical technique and judgement but it was “misunderstood” and opportunities to act on the findings were “missed”.

The winner of this non-entry category will be a businessperson from any sector who has made an outstanding and lasting contribution to sustainability, energy efficiency and net zero initiatives across the region. The winner will be selected by a panel of judges based on their expertise and industry insight. “RWE is proud to champion sustainability in East Anglia, and we want to see incredible examples of those committed to greener ways of working and encouraging others to do the same,” said Edward Robb, stakeholder manager at RWE. Edward Robb, stakeholder manager at RWE (Image: Edward Robb) Mr Robb explained that being a champion means prioritising sustainability in everything you do. “Going over and above to support local green spaces, working in sustainable ways, making efforts with recycling, using clean energy – these are just a few of the examples we want to see in this category!” Innovation is a key part of the award, with judges looking for individuals who pioneer new methods and technologies. “As a champion, others will look to you as a leader, and so being able to platform new sustainable innovations is incredibly valuable in this category,” Mr Robb said. “By showcasing these champions, we also raise the bar for the wider community for sustainability, community focus and green habits.” Standing out as a leader in clean and green business isn’t just beneficial for East Anglia’s business community though, it can also act as a badge of honour for growing enterprises. “This is a fantastic award to scream and shout about for your business or organisation, and something to be truly proud of,” said Mr Robb. “Being able to recognise these champions is truly an honour and gives them the recognition they deserve.” Submit your entries before the deadline on Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information about the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To read about all of the award categories, please click here. RWE is the leading power generator in the UK, with a diverse operational portfolio of onshore wind, offshore wind, solar, hydro, biomass and gas. These projects have a total planned capacity of 4.2 gigawatts, located 50 to 80km off the coast of Norfolk, and will generate enough clean energy to power more than 4 million UK homes. RWE directly employs around 3,200 people across the UK and its planned investments will continue to create new jobs, support communities and help develop skills up and down the country. RWE is committed to working in partnership with the government to help deliver its clean power ambitions, alongside secure and affordable energy for the UK. This non-entry category celebrates an individual who has made an outstanding and lasting contribution to advancing sustainability, energy efficiency and net zero initiatives in East Anglia. The winner may come from any sector and will have demonstrated leadership in both promoting and implementing clean and green practices.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Flight disruptions expected to continue at UK airports today after technical issues
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
Flight disruptions at UK airports are expected to continue on Wednesday (September 9) due to a technical issue affecting air traffic control services. NATS, which provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports, was hit by the issue on Tuesday (September 8). As a result, around 1,300 flights to and from UK airports were cancelled, according to flight monitoring website Flightradar24. Tens of thousands of passengers were caught up in cancellations and delays. Further disruptions are expected on Wednesday as airlines deal with the knock-on effects at major UK airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted. Travel journalist Simon Calder warned that the effects on Wednesday were “going to be horrible”. Mr Calder told Sky News: “There are going to be dozens of cancellations in the morning of flights coming into Heathrow because, basically, the flights didn’t go out tonight.” Heathrow Airport said its operations were “still recovering” after the technical issue. Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew.
    Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be… pic.twitter.com/DZ2g7GQYkL — Heathrow Airport (@HeathrowAirport) September 9, 2026 Its website said: "Flights are operating today, however some knock-on disruption is expected as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. "Passengers are advised to check the latest status of their flight directly with their airline and to only travel to Heathrow if their flight is confirmed as operating today. "We apologise to passengers affected by the disruption. "Additional colleagues are available across our terminals to provide support, and we are working closely with NATS and our airline partners to return operations to normal as quickly as possible." Manchester Airport has said it is back "operating as normal" following Tuesday's technical issues. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), the airport added: "Those travelling today should continue with their journey plans and check with their airline for the latest information on their flight, as usual. “Thank you for your patience and understanding.” ℹ️ Information for passengers - 09.09.26 | 7:30am pic.twitter.com/y1jeR2VvRD — Manchester Airport (@manairport) September 9, 2026 Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted and that it had cancelled more than 50 scheduled flights as a result of NATS' technical issues. British Airways said it had been forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday, affecting “tens of thousands of customers”. Some passengers were trapped on planes on runways for hours. NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe said he “always accept(s) full responsibility” when asked whether he was considering his position after the incident. Mr Rolfe told Sky News: “I am the CEO of a piece of critical infrastructure, so it is my job to take responsibility for that.” “What I absolutely take responsibility for is keeping people safe and delivering the best service we possibly can on a day like today.” “You will understand my focus is entirely about how we actually resolve this issue, get things back to normal, help our airlines, our airport customers and the travelling public.” But Mr Rolfe has faced criticism from Wizz Air and Ryanair following the latest problem. Ryanair’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, called for Mr Rolfe to resign. Mr McMahon said: “How many more failures do passengers have to suffer before overpaid failure Nats CEO Martin Rolfe accepts responsibility for his repeated mismanagement and resigns?” “Over three years after Nats’ catastrophic 2023 system meltdown, it’s clear that nothing has changed, with UK passengers once again suffering avoidable ATC (air traffic control) delays of up to eight hours today due a critical Nats ATC system failing.” Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander is due to speak with Mr Rolfe on Wednesday. She is also expected to address MPs in the Commons during the second reading of the Civil Aviation Bill. NATS, posting on X on Tuesday night, said it will work on assisting airlines and airports recover from Tuesday’s technical issues. It added: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” “We apologise again for the disruption caused. Passengers should check with their airline on the status of their flight tonight or tomorrow.” ℹ️ Technical issue
    Work is continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from today's disruption. This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover. (1/2) https://t.co/Me6GAY385V — NATS (@NATS) September 8, 2026 Cancelled flights can leave passengers entitled to care, refunds, alternative travel and, in some cases, compensation, the UK Civil Aviation Authority explains. Under UK law, airlines must provide food and drink, a way to communicate, accommodation and transport when a flight is cancelled. This applies until passengers reach their destination, regardless of the delay’s length or its cause. If passengers need to stay overnight, airlines may arrange a nearby hotel and transport. Where an airline cannot provide care during major disruption, passengers can organise reasonable assistance themselves and claim the money back. Passengers should keep every receipt and avoid spending more than necessary. Passengers may also qualify for compensation if they received less than 14 days’ notice. This does not usually apply when cancellation was caused by extreme weather, airport or air traffic control strikes, or another extraordinary circumstance. For cancellations notified seven to 14 days ahead, compensation may be: This depends on the delay at the final destination, with lower amounts for shorter delays. For notice of less than seven days, passengers may claim £220, £350, £520 or £260, depending on flight distance and delay. Passengers can choose a refund for unused travel or an alternative flight. They may ask about another airline or suitable transport if it would get them there significantly sooner. Has your flight been affected by Tuesday's technical issues? Let us know in the poll above or in the comments below.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire Combined authority to review e-vehicle safety
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More children are reportedly suffering more head injuries after falling from scooters, a Cambridgeshire councillor has claimed. The claim has been made as concerns have been raised over a contract to provide e-bikes and scooters across parts of the county. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority currently has a contract with Voi to provide e-bikes and e-scooters across Cambridge and some surrounding areas. They were introduced as part of a trial in 2020 which has since been extended until May 2028. It is illegal to ride a privately owned e-scooter in public – only those offered by Voi as part of the trial can be legally used in the city. But some councillors have raised concerns over the vehicles blocking pavements, cluttering public spaces and the safety of riders. The combined authority’s overview and scrutiny panel asked for a report on the “social value” of e-scooters and data on injuries. Cllr Anna Bradnam, of South Cambs District Council, said they had also asked for data on illegal scooters and e-bikes too. She also asked for information to be provided by organisations that deal with head and brain injuries such as Headway and children’s hospices. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “Coincidentally, I have visited a hospice and just asked them out of the blue – because the hospice deals with children with life-limiting and life-changing conditions – have you seen more children come in because of falling off scooters? “They said, ‘oh, yes’ – I was really quite surprised, but of course lots of people on scooters don’t wear helmets.” Cllr Hugh Clough, of Cambridge City Council, said Voi had not consulted them before deciding where to put designated drop-off points. The Green councillor said: “Voi’s actual responsiveness to concerns raised by the public and councillors is a major issue in our area. “The lack of any sort of willingness to engage with councillors – that problem was raised too many times. “We’ve all got the list of problem sites where people can’t get through, can’t get in – you can’t even get your mobility scooter or wheelchair through. It’s a festering problem which needs to be addressed.” Cllr Bradnam asked for the topic to be brought to the panel as part of the January 2027 agenda list.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Police failures contributed to murder of mother-of-three, inquest finds
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have been heavily criticised for failing to protect a Biggleswade mother-of-three who was murdered by her partner. Sarah Albone, 38, was killed by her partner Matthew Waddell, 35, who was jailed for life in September 2023 for her murder. Her body was found in February 2023, three months after she was last seen, concealed in a suitcase inside a wheelie bin. Matthew Waddell murdered Sarah Albone and is serving life in prison. (Image: Bedfordshire Police) An inquest has found that police failures in recognising and responding to escalating domestic abuse contributed to her death. Police had been called to her home several times from August 2021. Senior coroner Emma Whitting found that Sarah faced such an immediate risk in the 16 months before her murder that the state had a duty to protect her, but had failed to do so. Waddell’s campaign of abuse began after meeting Sarah in November 2020. She had multiple sclerosis and became dependent on him, despite ending the relationship multiple times. Waddell repeatedly returned to her home and ignored police bail conditions. Sarah had reported him to police for harassment and assault, detailing his controlling and aggressive behaviour. Waddell killed her in a violent attack before hiding her body and sending messages from her phone to mislead friends and family. He was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 32 years. The case also triggered a Domestic Homicide Review, which identified failings across multiple agencies and called for a more trauma-informed approach to supporting vulnerable victims. A post-mortem examination found the cause of Sarah's death was airway obstruction due to catastrophic head injuries. It is believed she died in November 2022. John Tizard, police and crime commissioner for Bedfordshire, said: "My thoughts remain with Sarah’s family and all those affected by this deeply tragic case. "This case happened four years ago and systems and processes have changed but all agencies involved must accept their responsibilities, apologise, and learn the lessons. "The Domestic Homicide Review identified a number of failings across agencies, including missed opportunities to recognise vulnerability and a lack of vigilance in adopting a trauma-informed approach. "I shall be seeking assurances from the police and the Chief Constable that the failings identified four years ago could not arise in the same way today, and that and that every possible step has been taken to prevent such failings from occurring again."

The issue is impacting flight departures from multiple airports, including Heathrow, Manchester and Edinburgh. NATS (National Air Traffic Services), the UK’s air traffic control provider, confirmed the problem and is currently working to resolve it.
  
  In an update to passengers, NATS said, "We are investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures." Here is a full list of all the airports facing delays and groundings: Around 200 flights were cancelled on Tuesday afternoon because of the air traffic control issue, with that number expected to rise, flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said. Heathrow Airport confirmed the disruption in a statement, emphasising that only departing flights are affected. A Heathrow spokesperson said: “The air traffic control service Nats is experiencing a technical issue which is impacting departing flights at UK airports. “Arriving flights are not currently impacted. “We are supporting our local Nats team in their efforts to resolve the issue as quickly as possible. “We will provide updated information when we have it.” Passengers have been advised to check with their airlines for the latest information before travelling to the airport. Heathrow apologised to affected customers and said it is supporting Nats in resolving the issue. Passengers have been advised to check the latest flight information with their airlines. It is understood that a fix is now in place. Have you been affected by the issue? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Kimbolton Castle to glow for East Anglian Air Ambulance
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Kimbolton Castle will light up in support of a lifesaving charity. The historic site will glow red or yellow on Wednesday, September 9, in support of the East Anglian Air Ambulance (EAAA) as part of a wider display during Air Ambulance Week, helping raise awareness of the charity’s emergency care work across the region. Matthew Jones, CEO at East Anglian Air Ambulance, said: "We're incredibly grateful to Kimbolton Castle, Huntingdon Town Hall, Cromwell Museum and Godmanchester Chinese Bridge for supporting Air Ambulance Week and helping us raise awareness of the work our crews do every day. "Seeing well-known buildings illuminated across the region is a powerful reminder of the difference local communities make in helping us continue to provide lifesaving care, whenever and wherever it's needed." Other landmarks taking part include Peterborough Cathedral, the Guildhall/Corn Exchange and the Grand Arcade in Cambridge. The show of support comes as EAAA continues to fundraise for its Cambridge Air Base Appeal. The charity must relocate its operations ahead of Cambridge Airport's closure in 2030 and has so far raised £3.6 million towards the new base, with a further £4.4 million still needed. Mr Jones said: "This is about more than lighting up a building or making a donation – it's our community coming together to protect the people we love and secure the future of the lifesaving care we deliver across the counties we serve." Will Chuter, headteacher at Kimbolton School, said: "We're proud to support East Anglian Air Ambulance during Air Ambulance Week. "Lighting up Kimbolton Castle is a simple but meaningful way to recognise the dedication of the charity's crews and to encourage people to learn more about the incredible work they do across our community." Without the new Cambridge facility, EAAA's operations would be cut in half, with the replacement base planned for land at New Shardelowes Farm near Fulbourn.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fire service to finally withdraw after 'extremely tough' Holme Fen blaze
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major fire at a Cambridgeshire nature reserve that burned for more than a month is now under control. The blaze broke out at Holme Fen Nature Reserve in Cambridgeshire on August 8, leading to a major incident being declared by Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. More than 100 firefighters and 20 fire engines responded to the scene at its peak. The blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 (Image: Emily Stevens) After 31 days at the site, firefighters will hand control back to Natural England this week. Stuart Smith, assistant chief fire officer, said: "This has been the biggest incident our county has faced in many, many years. "We have seen crews from every fire station attend at some point during the response, as well as the fantastic support we’ve received from our colleagues across the country through National Resilience arrangements. "It’s been an extremely tough incident, especially with the gruelling hot weather we’ve seen over the last month or so, but we have reached a point where we feel it is safe for us to withdraw all crews and hand the site back over to Natural England." The fire spread around a four-kilometre perimeter, covering an area equivalent to around 60 football pitches, and burned deep into the peat. Firefighters from across the UK, including Durham and Darlington, Devon and Somerset, and Merseyside, were called in to assist. Crew Manager Jake Banks was called in to assist (Image: Emily Stevens) During the second week, around 50 firefighters worked on site by day and 30 overnight to control the blaze and clear the area. By the third week, the major incident had been stood down and National Resilience crews had returned home, leaving Cambridgeshire firefighters to clear the site and tackle hotspots. Mr Smith said: "We’ve had outstanding support from many people and places throughout the incident, which we are extremely grateful for. "It's not just the front-facing firefighters, the work behind the scenes to manage an incident like this is phenomenal. "Our own officers, control operators, and support colleagues ensured those on site had everything they needed and that we could maintain emergency cover across the county for other incidents, plus our neighbouring fire and rescue services have been incredibly supportive in helping with that too. The fire at Holme Fen has been burning for a month (Image: Sinead Everett) "Partner agencies, particularly the Environment Agency and Middle Level Commissioners, have played a major role in ensuring we had water supplies. "We've needed road closures, had ambulance colleagues on standby and worked closely with Natural England and contractors on site, who have worked so hard, to help us bring this fire to a safe conclusion as quickly as possible." He also praised local farmers, businesses and others in the surrounding community for supporting crews during the incident. Mr Smith said: "The Rapid Relief Team, The Admiral Wells pub, Ramsey Town Council, and everyone who has supported their efforts to provide food for firefighters at the scene has been at the heart of the community response. "Thank you doesn't seem enough, but we are so grateful for the support everyone has given." More than 40 firefighters tackled the blaze at Holme Fen (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service) He said a full review will now take place to inform future responses. Mr Smith said: "The next steps are just as important for us as a fire and rescue service. "In the coming weeks, we will undergo a thorough debrief process. "This was an unprecedented fire for us and it is important we take time to reflect and note what went well and highlight where we could improve should we have another incident like this again. "We do this for all larger incidents and it’s an invaluable process to ensure we continue to be as prepared as we can be for incidents and share that learning internally and nationally in the sector." Managed by Natural England, Holme Fen covers 657 acres and is designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest, supporting a wide variety of wildlife.

A woman in her 20s was arrested over the incident and released on bail. Anyone with information can email Detective Constable Lewis Stanley at Lewis.Stanley@herts.police.uk. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire rowing club is generating its own electricity after installing solar panels. St Neots Rowing Club is generating renewable electricity with a new solar and battery-storage system. The Warwick and Dominey Fund, administered by the Cambridgeshire Community Foundation, gave the club a grant for the project. The 34-panel system stores excess electricity in batteries for later use. It is expected to produce about 15,000kWh of electricity a year. That is enough energy to boil more than 500,000 kettles. Machelec designed and installed the system in three days, causing minimal disruption to the club’s activities. The club said the project is a major step towards long-term sustainability and could unlock further investment. It could also help the club switch from petrol to electric launches, cutting emissions, noise and pollution. The club also thanked member Lillian for helping make the solar panels a reality. St Neots Rowing Club was also chosen as the first site for a trial of river-level sensors that can issue early flood warnings.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Councillor calls for more planning powers to protect high street diversity
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire councillor wants councils to be given more power to protect the mix of businesses on high streets. Reform councillor Karan Maheshwari, who represents Ramsey, has submitted a motion for debate at Huntingdonshire District Council’s meeting on Wednesday. The motion says planning rules give businesses flexibility but can leave councils powerless when one type of business dominates an area. Under current planning regulations, many businesses fall within Use Class E, which allows a range of commercial, business and service activities to switch between uses without requiring planning permission. Class E covers businesses including barbers, nail bars, beauty salons and mobile-phone sales and repair shops (Image: File image) Class E covers businesses including barbers, nail bars, beauty salons and mobile-phone sales and repair shops. The motion says the Government has already proposed planning permission for new vape shops and adult gaming centres. But it says similar concerns can arise when barbers, nail bars, beauty salons or mobile-phone shops become concentrated in a town centre. Cllr Maheshwari’s proposal says no lawful business should be judged simply by its type and that Class E businesses can benefit high streets. Read more Reform councillor tables motion to stop further asylum accommodation in Hunts Structural concerns spark refusal of home plan for former meat preparation store 5 of the best-rated places in Cambridgeshire for a Sunday roast Robotic mower named by pupil keeps primary school field tidy Heritage Open Day to shine spotlight on Alconbury's military past It says planning concerns arise only when “robust local evidence” shows that too many businesses of one type are harming an area’s diversity, vitality or viability. If approved, the council would ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government to consider powers allowing councils to require planning permission for future changes to a specific Class E use in a defined town-centre area. The powers would be used only where evidence shows that more businesses of one type are harming, or are likely to harm, a town centre’s character and economic health. The motion says new powers must preserve Class E’s flexibility, include safeguards and appeal rights, and rely on local evidence rather than blanket bans. If adopted, the council would send the motion to Huntingdonshire’s MPs and the Local Government Association for their support.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Reform councillor tables motion to stop further asylum accommodation in Hunts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A St Neots councillor will ask Huntingdonshire District Council to oppose any expansion of asylum accommodation and reject becoming a "Council of Sanctuary". Reform councillor Ricky Ioannides has tabled the motion for Wednesday’s full council meeting. The motion says immigration policy, asylum decisions and accommodation are matters for the Government and Home Office, but claims asylum housing can put pressure on homes, healthcare, policing and other local services. It states: "Huntingdonshire District Council does not consent to the further expansion of Home Office asylum accommodation within Huntingdonshire. "The council calls for an immediate moratorium on additional asylum accommodation capacity, for existing accommodation not to be renewed or replaced as contracts expire, and for the Home Office asylum accommodation estate within Huntingdonshire to be progressively reduced with the objective of ending its use within the district." If approved, the motion would put the council formally against any further expansion of Home Office asylum accommodation in Huntingdonshire. It would also say the district should not seek or support "Council of Sanctuary" status or anything similar. Councillors will be asked to back an immediate halt to any increase in asylum accommodation in the district. The proposal rules out new asylum hotels, more dispersed accommodation or additional homes, flats, HMOs and other premises for asylum use. The motion also calls on the Home Office and its contractors to let existing accommodation contracts expire without renewal or replacement, with the aim of ending asylum accommodation in Huntingdonshire. The council would not offer its land or property for asylum accommodation or promote Huntingdonshire as a site for future schemes. The motion also calls for the council to remove website wording saying it welcomes "asylum seekers, refugees and detainees" and replace it with politically neutral information on the roles of the council and Home Office. The motion also calls for regular reports to councillors on asylum property numbers and locations, the cost to council services and any expansion plans. The motion says it would not override the council’s legal duties, require unlawful discrimination or interfere with independent planning and regulatory decisions. If approved, the council’s executive leader would write to the Home Secretary, ministers, local MPs and Home Office accommodation providers to set out Huntingdonshire’s opposition to further expansion. National Home Office figures for June 2026 showed hotel placements had fallen by 50% year on year to 16,021, while dispersal accommodation increased by 4% to 69,038.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Plans for local government reorganisation in Cambs on hold as review launched
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Plans for local government reorganisation in Cambridgeshire are on hold due to new legal advice, the government has said. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said the review is to ensure the process is robust and aligns with the new Government’s aim to “rewire the state”, and follows “updated and privileged legal advice”. At least eight councils have launched legal challenges or were considering doing so due to opposition to the Government’s choice of footprints for new councils. Reform UK-led Kent County Council is set to consider a judicial review at a meeting on Tuesday after it did not receive a response from the Government to a letter setting out concerns. Plans for reorganisation in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn in the light of new legal advice. Decisions on 14 further areas will be reviewed and paused alongside the cases of Cambridgeshire & Peterborough and West Sussex, which are yet to have a decision confirmed. The Government will also confirm that local elections in May 2027 will go ahead on existing council boundaries, saying it remains committed to effective and sustainable local government and simplifying these structures. Communities Secretary Angela Rayner is expected to tell Parliament on Monday: “As we are now more determined than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent, it’s only right that as a new Secretary of State I make sure that everything we do is working towards that plan to change Britain, without delay. “The Prime Minister told the House last week he was ‘prepared to look at local government reorganisation’ and he asked me as his Communities Secretary to ‘do that’. “In that context, in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law. “And, secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new Prime Minister, and any additional considerations. “I do not take this lightly. I recognise the huge amount of work that has already gone into progressing reorganisation in each of these areas and I am very grateful for it.” MHCLG said reorganisation in Surrey will not be affected by the review and the two new unitary authorities, East and West Surrey, will go live in April 2027. Reform UK has claimed credit for the Government’s decision to halt the process, with the party leading county councils in Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex which all launched legal challenges to reorganisation. Reform leader Nigel Farage said: “Reform UK not only argued that this Government’s plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is. “Earlier this year we took on the Government and forced them to give the vote back to millions of people after Labour tried to cancel democracy. “Now, thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the Government has backed down on their plans yet again. “Only Reform had the backbone to stand up to these reckless plans. This is yet another embarrassing defeat for Labour. Only Reform backs real democracy.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Undercover investigation aired by Channel 4 a 'hoax', says Hunts Reform group
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Huntingdonshire Reform UK group has branded allegations over the party’s donations and vetting process a “hoax”. Two senior Reform officials stepped down on September 4 after Channel 4 aired an undercover investigation. Verbatim Investigations, founded by Centre for Climate Reporting journalists, filmed Nigel Farage and other Reform officials allegedly trying to bypass electoral law. Three influential opinion polls that made headlines for Reform before the May local elections were allegedly funded by a US company at the instruction of one of Mr Farage’s aides. However, the supposed donors behind the US company were actually undercover reporters. Footage shows Reform leader Mr Farage thanking the undercover reporters after the polls were published in May. Foreign donations are tightly regulated in the UK, and Mr Farage admitted to the BBC that the situation “looks bad”. Cllr Peter Gammons, of the Huntingdonshire Reform group, said: "Reform UK has been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. "The party denies any wrongdoing." Cllr Gammons said Reform was launching an internal investigation into the broadcast. He also questioned Verbatim Investigations’ credibility. Cllr Gammons said: "This is yet another establishment attack on Reform UK." The two officials were Reform's head of policy James Orr and long-serving Nigel Farage aide Dan Jukes. The Electoral Commission said it was considering all relevant information and had contacted the Metropolitan Police.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Call for Huntingdonshire draft Local Plan decision to be delayed amid concerns
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Residents have raised serious concerns about Huntingdonshire District Council’s draft Local Plan ahead of a key vote this week. More than 1,000 residents responded to a North Huntingdon & St Ives Cumulative Impacts Group survey, revealing widespread opposition to the plan’s evidence and proposed growth. More than 90 per cent said they did not trust the Local Plan’s evidence, while 93 per cent said it should not be finalised until clearer evidence was available. Around 60 per cent opposed the proposed growth, while 33 per cent backed development in principle but not at the draft’s scale. Only around 5 per cent supported the targets. Read more Reform councillor tables motion to stop further asylum accommodation in Hunts Further details emerge after police rush to Huntingdonshire bus station Structural concerns spark refusal of home plan for former meat preparation store 5 of the best-rated places in Cambridgeshire for a Sunday roast Hunts council motion to remove support from controversial car park plans Infrastructure was a major concern, with around 80 per cent worried about road congestion and almost 70 per cent concerned about water and wastewater capacity. Another 63 per cent highlighted pressure on schools and healthcare, along with the impact on the countryside and farmland. The survey closed as Huntingdonshire District Council’s overview and scrutiny panel for performance and growth met last week. Councillors reviewed the early findings and recommended that Cabinet and then Full Council consider the draft Local Plan on Wednesday (9). A survey carried out by the North Huntingdon & St Ives Cumulative Impacts Group attracted more than 1,000 responses from residents across the district and found widespread opposition to the evidence underpinning the plan and the scale of growth proposed. (Image: Huntingdonshire District Council) Officers acknowledge the widespread concern but are recommending approval for the plan, warning that delay or abandonment would restart the process and risk government intervention. A report says there are “no circumstances” to justify departing from the Government’s standard method for calculating housing need, so the overall requirement remains unchanged. Campaigners argue that the planning landscape changed after the new National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) was published in August 2026. The council can complete the plan under the previous framework, but campaigners say decisions made after adoption will be judged under the new national rules. The group also questions changes since earlier versions, including lower affordable-housing requirements, looser specialist and accessible-housing policies, a cut in self-build provision from five per cent to zero and biodiversity net gain reduced from 20 per cent to the statutory minimum of 10 per cent. Campaigners are particularly concerned about growth around Lodge Farm and Wyton Airfield, described in council documents as a “substantial new urban community”, according to the group’s statement. Campaigners say the council has not yet published a cumulative infrastructure assessment. Paul Boothman, chair of the North Huntingdon & St Ives Cumulative Impacts Group, said: "The survey shows overwhelming doubt in the evidence base and serious concern about infrastructure capacity. "Residents are asking councillors to look closely at these shortcomings and to test whether the plan is genuinely ready. "This decision cannot be made on assumptions - it needs clear answers." Campaigners say key questions remain over whether the plan will comply with the new national rules, whether infrastructure can keep pace, whether water-use assumptions are realistic and whether major growth areas have been assessed together. If full council approves it, the draft Local Plan will enter a six-week Regulation 19 consultation from mid-September to October, giving residents and organisations a final chance to make formal representations before examination by a planning inspector. The draft plan includes 24,000 homes, more than double the current housing stock in Huntingdon, which has about 10,000 homes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New 20mph limits in Cambridgeshire have reduced driver speeds, report shows
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A county council report revealed new 20mph limits on roads have shown “statistically significant” drops in speed a year after being introduced. Cambridgeshire County Council began introducing the new limits across the county from early 2024, across a total of 25 roads so far. The report, presented to the council’s highways and transport committee on Tuesday (September 1), looked at the impact of the limit on eight of these roads within the first year. It found that average speed was reduced on all of them. It looked at schemes in Cambourne, Histon, Ely, Great Abington, Fowlmere, Ramsey, St Neots, and Great Staughton. Speed reductions ranged from six per cent to 16 per cent, with the largest falls seen where speeds were highest before the limit was introduced. The report said early evidence of the limit’s impact on crashes is “encouraging but remains inconclusive” as numbers were already low in many towns. It said Ely is the only location which has so far shown a statistically significant fall in crashes, but Cambourne, Histon, and Ramsey have shown a downward trend. The report said there were an average of 15.6 crashes per year in Ely across the seven years from 2017, but this fell by nearly half in the scheme’s first year. It said there were eight crashes after the limit’s introduction, which was a “notable reduction” as crashes across Cambridgeshire had only fallen by 12 per cent. In St Neots, crashes actually increased during the first year but the report said this was not significant and falls within normal annual variation. It added that evaluating the scheme’s impact on crash rates will need at least three years of data, and recommended a further review at a later stage. The council collected anonymous data through sensors to determine speed and police road traffic collision records for crashes. The council has set aside £150,000 per year for new 20mph schemes with more currently planned or delivered in another 29 locations.
